abstract: IMS (the IP Multimedia Subsystem) is one of the principal components in the evolution of the control plane as fixed and mobile networks migrate to IP. The Service Delivery Platform (SDP) is the basis for value added services, such as multi-media content and games. The IMS is specified by ETSI/3GPP standards, while the SDP has emerged as a pragmatic approach within the industry. This presentation describes how IMS and the SDP combine to deliver new services. It describes the technical and business challenges that operators face in deploying a new service plane. It uses operator case studies to highlight key points. Finally it looks at how emerging Web 2.0 technology will affect the NGN.

abstract: N3 is the broadband network that connects the NHS in England and most sites in Scotland. Early in 2007, BT, as the N3 Service Provider, delivered the English network two months ahead of schedule. With over 20,000 connections, N3 is already one of Europe’s largest, secure, VPN networks. N3 will become one of the largest converged private networks in the world, carrying multimedia applications across the NHS at speeds of up to 100Mbps. And the journey has only just begun. Late in 2006 the network was upgraded to support 6-Layer Quality of Service (QoS) and in July 2007 N3SP formally launched N3 Voice Services based on Voice over IP. There is much more to come from one of the most advanced public sector networks in the world serving 1.4 million users.

abstract: The UK is in a relatively strong position with respect to today’s broadband services to customers. However, the move to next generation access networks is continuing internationally, with announcements from a range of providers. These announcements have been made for a number of different reasons — this means that the situation for next generation access in different countries is likely to show significant variation. Despite this, it is important that the regy approaches to next generation access are clearly articulated, to avoid the risk of inefficient delays to investment. It is for this reason that Ofcom has recently consulted on the principles and a number of specific approaches that could be adopted in respect of next generation access networks where such regulation is necessary.

abstract: Four years ago Vodafone initiated a project to enable WiFi hotspot access for their customers. The requirement was to roam on to third party networks rather than building our own hotspots. Customers should be able to gain access either using a web browser and SMS authentication, or a dedicated client and SIM authentication. Settlement within the group was based on RADIUS to TAP mediation, using existing settlement processes. At peak, 25 operating companies launched the product, of which eight were linked for roaming and TAP settlement.

abstract: Disappearing barriers in the telecom industry, fertile application innovation and rabid competition have created a new breed of players in our industry: Digital Service Providers. Reliant on next generation broadband networks, these new DSPs not only stimulate broadband consumption and use network capacity but also sometimes offer voice/messaging services and broadband for free. How to compete? Traditional operators must exploit their key competencies within an increasingly broad and complex value chain in which conventional “telecom” services are increasingly taken for granted. The session will explore the potential to build businesses on such core platforms as: - Customer base/mix of customers; - Customer info (preferences, behaviour) - Network delivery and therefore ad distribution capability to multiple screens - Ownership of media inventory online, on mobile portals and increasingly on IPTV; - Customer Services; - Payment/Billing relationship

abstract: Last year at this event, PBB-TE (then PBT) was new; this contribution will therefore open with a brief review of progress since then, in terms of standardisation, multi-vendor interoperability testing, and deployment. We will then consider what other connectivity models can be created by extending the PBB-TE paradigm, and placing Ethernet forwarding hardware under non-bridging control capabilities.

abstract: This final talk of the day looks at ideas for future next generation networks based on technologies yet to be established in both fixed and mobile networks. It will also identify areas where the technology needs to do more to meet operator and ultimately, end user needs. The scope of the talk will be from customer premises equipment to the network core.
